Generally the seeding shall be performed by use of acceptable commercial-type grain drills. If, in the opinion of the officer in charge, the soils are too loose or the area is too trashy to obtain satisfactory seeding by use of drills, he may authorize the use of acceptable commercial-type fertilizer spreaders, power broadcasters or other suitable broadcast seeding equipment. Also, should the plowing operations be completed at a time unfavorable to the seeding operations, the officer in charge may require the seeding to performed as a separate operation at a more favorable time. In either case the method and time of seeding shall be determined by the officer in charge. Any and all seeding equipment used must be supported by adequate hoppers, agitators, and controls to satisfactorily plant seed at a uniform rate and at an average depth of one-half inch to one inch.

Seedbeds shall be solid seeded except for omission of rock outcrops, deep washes, or steep slopes as determined by the officer in charge. The seed for the most part will be Crested Wheatgrass seed seeded at the approximate rate of five pound per acre with the understanding that sufficient Alfalfa seed may be added to form a mixture if determined advisable by the officer in charge which will thereby increase the rate of seeding to approximately six pounds per acre.

Seed at the rate per acre specified will be furnished by the Government.

The contractor shall be responsible for the delivery of the seed to the project site from the Government warehouse located in Burley, Idaho and for the protection of the seed from theft and weather while en route to, and from, and at the project site. Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Objectives and Results
1. Greater than 50% of seeded species basal gaps are =100cm. Conduct Drill Row Basal
Gap Intercept monitoring to determine seedling establishment success.
The drill row basal gap intercept method presented in the plan has been discontinued. However
the basal gap can be used as an indicator of perennial vegetation basal gap size. See results from
Objective 3 below.
2. A 20% increase in foliar cover of desirable perennial vegetation, and a 20% decrease in
invasive exotic annual vegetation compared to control plot (burned, untreated area).
Conduct Line Point Intercept monitoring to determine species cover/composition. (This
will only be conducted years 2 and 3.)
This objective was not met in 2017. Foliar cover for plots drill seeded with depth bands was
74.7% and 84% for plots drill seeded without depth bands, while foliar cover for control plots
was 69.2%. Average percent cover for cheatgrass was lower in all seeded plots compared to the
control plots. All seeded plots have a higher average percent cover for Sandberg bluegrass
compared to the control plot (Table 8-4).
Plots seeded with a standard drill with depth bands had the highest desirable perennial foliar
cover percentage (23.5%) compared to the control plots (13.6%). Desirable perennial foliar cover
in the minimum till plot at 17.7% was lowest compared to the other seeded plot types (Table 8-
4). The plots drill seeded with depth bands had the highest number of desirable perennials
present at each plot with 6 perennial species, compared to the control plots with 5 species, the
minimum till plots with 3, and the plots drill seeded without depth bands with 2 species. Out of
all desirable perennial species, Sandberg bluegrass was found at all 4 plot types.
Exotic annual cover was the highest at the plots seeded without depth bands (97.3%) and lowest
at the plots seeded with depth bands (68.3%). The dominant exotic annual plants were
cheatgrass, bur buttercup, and clasping pepperweed. Cheatgrass cover was the highest in the
control plots (51%); bur buttercup was highest in the minimum till plots (52%); clasping
pepperweed was highest in the drill seeded plots with depth bands (36.9%) (Table 8-4).
Foliar cover of drill-seeded species in plots drill seeded with Mix 1(Snake River wheatgrass and
bluebunch wheatgrass) was 4.7%, 6.2% for plots drilled with depth bands and seeded with Mix 2
(Snake River wheatgrass and bottlebrush squirreltail), and 0% for sites drilled without depth
bands and seeded with Mix 3.
3. 30% decrease in perennial vegetation basal gaps >50cm compared to control plot.
Conduct Basal Gap Intercept monitoring.
The objective was not met in 2017 as basal gaps over 50cm were not 30% lower in treated (drill
seeded) versus control plots. There was an average 2.2% decrease in gaps greater than 50cm in
treated areas compared to the control plots. There were also fewer basal gaps in treatment areas
than control plots.
The drill seeded areas were found to have the lowest percent of gaps of 50cm or more in 2015.
For example, in 2015, areas seeded with the standard drill with depth bands had the lowest
percentage of basal gaps at 74.3%, about 17% less gaps than the control plots. In 2017 the areas
seeded with the standard drill without depth bands had the lowest percentage at 88.4%, only
about 7% less gaps than the control plots.
There was an approximately 3% increase of basal gaps (>50cm) in the minimum till treatment
area and about 8% increase in the plots seeded with a standard drill with depth bands from 2014
to 2017. In the same dataset there was a decrease of about 2% in plots seeded with a standard
drill without depth bands. Since 2013, the total basal gap percentage for gaps greater than 50cm
increased consistently by approximately 2% per year. There was a 3% increase from 2015 to
2017 probably due to the longer time interval.
Overall, the percentage of basal gaps greater than 50cm appears to follow an marginally
increased in all treatments, with the exception of the 2015 season when it decreased slightly.
The trend is more obvious in the control plots as mentioned above. Even though this is true, the
treated areas still have lower basal gap percentages than the control plots.

In 2022 a qualitative site assessment of the one plot in Mix 2 north of Old Oregon Trail Road, G1MCT01, recorded Siberian wheatgrass as the dominant vegetation, Snake River wheatgrass subdominant with bottlebrush squirreltail and Sandberg bluegrass both minor components. Species richness was low at this plot with two seeded species, three native species, and three non-native annual forbs present.
The Mix 2 drill seeding south of Old Oregon Trail Road was a failure. Bur buttercup and clasping pepperweed dominated the entire treatment area with only a trace of bluebunch wheatgrass. This area is in the Mountain Home Subunit allotment Pasture 15 with April 1 to June 30, and November 1 to December 31 grazing. Vegetation surveys prior to the fire described the entire area as “heavily disturbed” with cheatgrass, bur buttercup, and clasping pepperweed.
The drill seeding likely failed in this area due to no seed bed preparation to decrease these invasive annuals, substantial drought the summer following the drill seeding, and very flat terrain with little to no micro-topography. The minor abundance of bunch grasses observed in 2017, bluebunch wheatgrass, Sandberg bluegrass, and Siberian wheatgrass are now absent.
If you were only to visit the treatment plots within Mix 1, no-till drill treatment your would think the drill seeding was a failure. Photos from the west side of the treatment area paint a different picture with patches of the drill seeding being successful. The majority of the area surrounding the plots is dominated by bur buttercup and clasping pepperweed with very few drill seeded species. Photos below were taken from the west side of the Mix 1 treatment area within a small dry drainage that provides micro-topography of east and southeast slopes and deep soils.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
On May 13, 1946, I inspected the range reseeding around Owinza Butte
made in the fall of 1945 on the Russell Fire burn.
Due to the fact that you can drive all over the reseeding area I was
able to make a very thorough inspection and check on all sites and exposures .
Small crested wheat seedlings were abundant along the drill rows and would
average 2- 3 inches in height over the whole area. The stand appeared to be
quite uniform throughout and there didn't seen to be a great deal of difference
between various sites and exposures . The poorest part of the stand that I found
was along the north side against the old blow out and dune area. The cheatgrass
was also the most abundant here and wherever the cheatgrass seedlings were thick
there seemed to be a very poor stand of crested wheat. However, most of the area
will not have cheatgrass on it this year and the crested wheat should be well
enough established by another year to withstand the competition.
After examining the whole area I came to the conclusion that we had a good
stand in view, of the adverse conditions of the seed bed last fall and the high
wind velocity in the area. At times last fall it was impossible to work in the
area due to dust. At the present time the area is beginning to blow badly again
due to the long dry spell. As a result some of the seedlings are beginning to
brown and will suffer from wind erosion. A good rain at this time would really
help this stand.
I found only one sign of trespass on the area since it was posted this spring.
A sheep wagon had crossed the southeast corner, but there seemed to be no sign of
any grazing on the posted area.
Mark E. Lawrence,
Range Examiner

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Rationale:  Establishment of a desirable perennial plant community that more closely matches the structural, species composition and diversity of the indigenous native plant community would help achieve a healthy, functioning rangeland, significantly reduce the potential for spread of invasive annual grasses and noxious weeds, and substantially diminish and control soil erosion affects across the watershed.

Accelerating the rate of reestablishment of native grasses, forbs and sagebrush is important to maintaining the value of the area as mule deer winter range, sage grouse breeding and wintering habitat.  Native seed mixtures are also an important component of suitable habitat for a number of Sensitive sagebrush obligate species.

Seed Mix #2:
The purpose of this seed mix is the same as above except that the seed mix is more conducive and better suited for the environmental and soil characteristics (range sites) encountered in this part of the burn.

The purpose of this seed mix is to restore and recover as quickly as possible some of the more sandier soil areas in the northern portion of the burn with a very adaptive, drought hardy and good diversity native and non-native plants that will replenish and refurbish deteriorating rangeland areas where many older rangeland seedings have occurred and some native vegetation sites have lost their sustainability, been depleted in composition and productive due to droughts, insects, grazing and other fires in the past, and lost much of their essential soil stability capabilities as perennial plants have weaken over time and, in some instances, have been gradually replaced with annual weed forms such as cheatgrass, bur buttercup and mustards.  If weather conditions are favorable for the next few years, the seeding of this mixture will provide a persistent and sustaining ground cover for the protection and benefit of the soils and the watershed, and improve habitat and food source conditions for wildlife and livestock.

Sandberg bluegrass and sand dropseed are both native, perennial grasses that are known to occur in these sandy sites and do well in this particular precipitation zone.  Both should do well here.  The non-native Siberian wheatgrass is particularly favored in this area because of it ability to compete with the higher levels of cheatgrass found here.  Also it has a very successful germination and survival rate compared to other species here, especially some natives, it is very drought tolerant, and it is has good soil binding and stability qualities.  Although alfalfa is the only proposed forb, it purpose it aid as a nitrogen fixer in the soil for the benefit of other plants of the area, plus it provides a good ground cover and forage for wildlife and livestock.

The reason other native forbs (i.e., Lomatium spp, Antennaria spp, Erigeron spp, Lithophragma spp, Crepis spp, Phlox spp, Allium spp.) is not available commercially&* and other forbs such as globemallows (Sphaeralcea spp.) and breadtongue Penstemon are available in limited quantities, and at very high costs.  A few other native forbs (i.e., Balsamorhiza spp., Agoseris spp.) have had little or no success when drill or aerial seeded with other species.

Rationale:  Establishment of a desirable perennial plant community that more closely matches the structural, species composition and diversity of the indigenous native plant community would help achieve a healthy, functioning rangeland, significantly reduce the potential for spread of invasive annual grasses and noxious weeds, and substantially diminish and control soil erosion affects across the watershed.

Accelerating the rate of reestablishment of native grasses, forbs and sagebrush is important to maintaining the value of the area as mule deer winter range, sage grouse breeding and wintering habitat.  Native seed mixtures are also an important component of suitable habitat for a number of Sensitive sagebrush obligate species.

Seed Mixes #9 and #10:
These mixes would be the subject of high-level monitoring to evaluate two important native grass species, Indian ricegrass and Needle-and-thread, in their ability to germinate, survive, endure, spread, mix with other native plants of the area, provide the intended soil stabilization necessary and become highly productive over a long period of time in these sandy soil areas within the exclosures.  If successful, future seedings with these particular species in sandy soil environments would be proposed depending on the response of these test sites.  Additional watershed and wildlife benefits are also anticipated.  These exclosure sites are part of the high-level monitoring described in the monitoring plan in Part 6.  The purpose of this action is to produce data evaluating the effectiveness of these treatments in order to save time and money in the future.

Objectives: To establish a desirable perennial plant community that would help achieve a healthy, functioning rangeland and significantly reduce the potential for spread of invasive annual grasses and noxious weeds.
Planned_Implementation:
Approximately 3,525 acres of the burned area would be drill seeded with a mix of up to four
native perennial grass species and two to three native perennial forb species, depending upon
funding and seed availability, at a rate of 10.375 lbs per acre. The treatment would be
completed in fall 2012 (FY2013) using leased tractors and BLM drills. In addition to the
3,525 acres of native grass and forb seeding, 440 acres would be drill seeded with a mix
of Wyoming and basin big sagebrush at a rate of 1.0 pound per acre using a Truax\xae drill
owned by the BLM and a leased tractor. The drill would be set up to plant seed at a very
shallow depth and then pressed into the soil with rollers attached to the drill. This method
has been very successful in the past and would put the seeds at the proper depth in the soil
and maximize the seed-to-soil contact. This method would apply about 279,000 pure live
seeds per acre on the treated area. The treatment area would be drilled in long narrow strips
spaced approximately 200 feet apart throughout the designated seeding boundary following
Cox's Well - G1Q8 - 08/02/2012 - Page 10 of 30
the initial grass and fob seeding, and would be less than ten percent of the BLM burned area.
Prior to any of the drill seeding treatments, areas identified would be inventoried for cultural
resources and flagged (or re-flagged in areas that have been previously inventoried) to
prevent undue damage to cultural resources during the seeding treatments. Figure 2 displays
the areas to be seeded.
Actual_Implementation: Drill seeding was completed by both field office and district crews. 2,500 acres were seeded with native perennial grasses, forbs and shrubs using standard rangeland drills and rented tractors. Sagebrush was also seeded, however due to the limited quantity of seed received; the Truax\xae seeding method was rejected in favor of a UTV, whirlybird and harrow. FY13 funds were used to cover the implementation of the seeding treatment including tractor rental, drill FOR, labor, camp rate, parts, fuel and seed mixing. Based upon the reduced funds received during FY13, only about $43k was allocated to this action.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
A native seed mix consisting of bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata), Snake River wheatgrass (Elymus wawawaiensis), basin wildrye (Leymus cinereus), Indian ricegrass (Achnatherum hymenoides), Thurber's needlegrass (Achnatherum thurberianum), big bluegrass (Poa ampla), Arrowleaf balsamroot (Balsamorhiza sagittata), blue flax (Linum perenne), and antelope bitterbrush (Purshia tridentata) was drilled at a rate of 8-10 lbs. per acre.  Total area treated within the burn was calculated to be approximately 2,500 acres.  Initially, the plan was to seed approximately 3,500 acres, however due to increased seed costs during the 2012 seed buy this acreage figure needed to be decreased.

A total of 15 sites were chosen to be monitored within the Cox’s Well Fire.  Sites were randomly generated in ArcMap based upon geographic features, range sites, and land treatment(s), and were validated in the field to ensure that the monitoring points represent the overall site conditions found within the project area.  Six (6) sites were selected within the seeded area of the burn, four (4) sites were in the burn but outside any of the treatment polygons, and five (5) sites were selected as control plots located outside the fire perimeter.  Sites were used to determine the vegetative density and cover in both seeded and unseeded areas and to determine the success or failure of the seeding and natural rehabilitation over the next three years.

Monitoring results for 2014 indicate that drill seeded areas averaged approximately 99,418 stems per acre (25 stems per meter\xb2) of seeded and existing perennial grasses.  This is a decrease of 61% compared to last year’s values of approximately 254,952 stems per acre.  Compared to those areas that were not treated, seeded areas only yielded 18% more perennial grass stems per m\xb2.  While this difference is substantially different than what was initially observed in 2013, the slight increase in perennial grass densities should correlate to increased cover in the coming years as those seedlings mature, should they survive.

As was the case in 2013, 2014 monitoring also revealed higher concentrations of cheatgrass stems per m\xb2 in unseeded areas than seeded areas.  Approximately 88% fewer cheatgrass stems per m\xb2 were encountered in the seeded areas compared to the unseeded areas.  Table 1 depicts the 2014 monitoring results of the vegetation cover found within the treated, untreated and unburned portions of the Cox’s Well Fire, while Figure 1 depicts the distribution of total vegetative cover in relation to total perennial cover during 2014 as well as how it compared to the 2013 values.  Table 2 depicts the 2014 density measurements for the native seeding in relation to the untreated areas within the burn, while Figure 2 shows the success of the seeding and the visual change in vegetative cover between monitoring years 2013 and 2014.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Objectives and Results
1. >50% of seeded species basal gaps are =100cm. Conduct drill row basal gap intercept
monitoring to determine seedling establishment success (Only conducted in Year 1).
This method was only conducted in 2012 (the year following the seeding). Due to timing and
funding constraints drill row monitoring was not conducted in 2013. These metrics were also not
measured in 2014 due to 1) difficulty finding previous drill row plots and 2) questionable
selection of drill plot locations by monitoring crews in 2012. Therefore, no data specific to drill
rows are available, so overall treatment success is evaluated using objectives 2-4 and other site
assessment information.
2. 20% increase in foliar cover of desirable perennial vegetation, and 20% decrease in
invasive exotic annual vegetation compared to control plot (burned and not drill seeded).
Conduct line point intercept monitoring to determine species cover/composition. (This
will only be conducted in years 2 and 3.)

In 2017, drill seeded plots had 21.3% greater foliar cover of desirable perennial vegetation than
the untreated plot outside of the exclosure. The average percent foliar cover of exotic annual
vegetation was 15.4% higher in that untreated plot compared to the drill seeded plots. Within the
exclosure, the drill seeded plot had a 21.9% higher average percent foliar cover for desirable
perennial vegetation than the non-drill seeded plot. The non-drill seeded plot also had 38%
higher average foliar cover of exotic annual vegetation (Figure 8-1, 8-2 and Table 8-2).
Since 2015, there was a 40% increase in percent foliar cover of exotic annual vegetation in the
non-drill seeded plot within the exclosure. There was a 6.7% increase in foliar cover of exotic
vegetation in the drill seeded plots. This objective has been met.
Siberian wheatgrass (Agropyron fragile) comprises the majority of the foliar cover at the drill seeded
plots (41%) and the control drill seeded plot (51%). Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda)
comprises the majority of the foliar cover at the control plot that was not drill seeded within the
exclosure (50.7%) and the plot in the untreated area outside the exclosure (48%) (Figure 8-1, 8-2
and Table 8-2).

3. 30% decrease in perennial vegetation basal gaps >50cm compared to control plot.
Conduct basal gap intercept monitoring.
In 2017, basal gaps greater than 50 cm were higher in the non-drill seeded plots compared to the
drill seeded plots; this difference was only 6% therefore, this objective was not met in 2017
4. Qualitative increase in perennial grass and forb diversity compared to control area.
Conduct line point intercept monitoring and site assessments.
Site assessments and photos from 2017 indicate there was an increase in perennial forb diversity
in the drill seeded plots compared to the control plot.
Both the drill seeded and non-drill seeded plots within the exclosure (G4ZNC01 and G4ZNC02),
the untreated plot outside the exclosure (G4ZNNT01), and all of the drill seeded plots except
G4ZNT02, had three perennial grass species. Plot G4ZNT02 had two perennial grass species.
Siberian wheatgrass (Agropyron fragile) was dominant (40-100% composition) within all of the
drill seeded plots except for G4ZNT04 where it was subdominant (10-40% composition).
Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda) was dominant at the untreated plot outside the exclosure
(G4ZNNT01) and subdominant at the drill seeded plots and at the non-drill seeded plot within
the exclosure. Bottlebrush squirreltail (Elymus elymoides) was subdominant at G4ZNNT01 and
drill seeded plot G4ZNT03, minor (2-10% composition) at the non-drill seeded plot within the
exclosure, and trace (<2%) at the drill seeded plot within the exclosure and drill seeded plots
G4ZNT01 and G4ZNT04. The drill seeded plots had more perennial forb diversity compared to
the drill seeded and non-drill seeded plots within the exclosure. Trace amounts of fleabane
(Erigeron) were noted at the drill seeded plot within the exclosure. Trace amounts of longleaf
phlox (Phlox longifolia) were found at drill seeded plots G4ZNT01 and G4ZNT03. Trace
amounts of larkspur (Delphinium sp.) were found at control plot G4ZNC01.
Comparing the non-drill seeded and drill seeded plots within the exclosure to the untreated plot
outside the exclosure, G4ZNC01 and G4ZNC02 both had subdominant amounts of Sandberg
bluegrass compared to G4ZNNT01 which had dominant. The percent cover of Siberian
wheatgrass was highest at the drill seeded plot within the exclosure (G4ZNC02).

Qualitative observations the first growing season showed fair to good

were established and quantitative data will be collected in FY 08. Photos were taken at each plot.

transects will be read in FY 08 at each plot location. Qualitative observations showed fair to
good germination of the drill seeded species. Spring moisture was below normal levels.

successful. Quantitative information will be collected in FY 08.

Objectives:
The objective of this treatment is to
establish a desirable perennial plant community that would help achieve a healthy, functioning rangeland and
significantly reduce the potential for spread invasive annual grasses and noxious weeds and mitigate soil erosion
impacts. The wildfire removed the majority of existing plant cover making the burn area more susceptible to
expansion of these plants. Natural recovery of native vegetation is not possible given pre-burn vegetative
conditions in the area. Establishment of perennial herbaceous species will enhance sage grouse nesting and
winter range habitat in the long term.
Planned_Implementation:
The burned pastures within the Neck, Tikura and Timmerman Hills
allotments would be drill seeded in the fall of 2008. The
proposed drill seeding area is approximately 7,872 acres. Approximately 70% or 5,500 acres would actually be
drill seeded in the area due to the presence of rock outcrops and unburned islands. A standard rangeland drill and
rubber tired tractor would be utilized for the seeding treatment.
Actual_Implementation:
Nature Drill Seeding
This project consisted of drill seeding approximately 5,684 acres out of a 14,868 acre area within
the Nature fire. Seed was applied in dry conditions at the beginning to wet ground later in the
process. The drill seeding was completed
by ESR staff and Fire Crew. Nine rangeland drills were used. The seed was premixed by ESR
Staff and Fire Crew. The project was started on October 14, 2008 and completed on November
18, 2008.

Seed Cost: $368,012.50
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Initial observations the first growing season showed good germination of the seeded grasses and forbs throughout the treatment area. Quantitative monitoring plots were established in FY09.
Monitoring Results FY09
Preliminary monitoring was established on the Nature fire. Qualitative and quantitative
observations gathered at the established plots showed good establishment of drilled seeded grass
and forb species. A cool and wet June contributed to the early establishment of seeded species. Bare ground across all plots averaged 35%. Density data reveals that seeded species are
currently below quantifiable objectives.

Objectives: Goal: Establish desirable perennial grass/forb plant community to provide critical forage for sage-grouse, big game\r\nspecies and preservation and maintenance of slickspots.
Planned_Implementation: Approximately 2,938 acres of the burned area would be drill seeded with perennial grass species adapted to the ecological sites. The two species will be drill seeded in alternate seed carts in a three drill cart configuration. The Siberian wheatgrass will be in two out of three drills covering 2/3 of the seeding area at a rate of 15 bulk pounds (12.1 PLS pounds), which is 61.2 seeds per square foot. The Snake River wheatgrass will be in one out of the three drills covering 1/3 of the area at a rate of 15 bulk pounds (11.5 PLS pounds), which is 44.8 seed per square foot. The total seeds per square foot for ground and aerial seeding within\r\nthe aerial strips is a maximum of 70.1 seeds per square foot. ESR Topic Guidelines are to limit seeding rates in combination to fewer than 80 seeds per square foot.
Actual_Implementation: Force Account - standard rangeland drill, 2,836* acres in\r\nOctober 2012
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2017: Results and Objective(s)
1. >50% of seeded species basal gaps are =100cm. Conduct drill row basal gap intercept
monitoring.
The drill row basal gap intercept method presented in the plan has been discontinued.

2. 20% increase in foliar cover of desirable perennial vegetation, and 20% decrease in
exotic annual vegetation compared to control plot (burned, untreated area). Conduct line
point intercept monitoring (only in years 2 and 3).
In 2017, the seeding did not meet foliar cover objectives. Foliar cover of desirable perennial
vegetation was 1.9% higher and exotic annual vegetation was higher by 58.9% in the natural
recovery plot compared to the drill seeded plots (Figure 8-1, photos below and Table 8-3). The
natural recovery plot was dominated by medusahead wildrye (Taeniatherum caput-medusae) and
cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) with desert parsley (Lomatium sp.). Total desirable perennial
vegetation was 20%. Drill seeded species were producing seedheads; however, cheatgrass and
medusahead were dominant elements of the species composition. Plots in the drill seeding
averaged over 100% foliar cover of exotic annual species foliar cover due to the multilayered
canopy of medusahead and cheatgrass. Plot G1UMT06 had the highest cover of desirable
perennial species and the highest cover of exotic annual species in 2017.

3. 30% decrease in perennial vegetation basal gaps > 50cm compared to control plot.
Conduct basal gap intercept monitoring. (Jornada “Monitoring Manual for Grassland,
Shrubland and Savanna Ecosystems” (Herrick et al. 2009))
In 2017, the average basal gap of drill seeded plots was similar to the natural recovery plot;
therefore, the objective of 30% fewer gaps >50cm in drill seeded area compared to control plots
has not been met. Both had an average of close to 15% for gaps smaller than 50cm and around
85% for gaps greater than 200cm. There was a difference in basal gaps between the drill seeded
plots. Plot G1UMT06 has fewer gaps above 200cm than other areas, 48.9% greater than 200cm
and 17% less than 50cm (Table 8-4). Siberian wheatgrass was observed as dominant and healthy
in the drill rows (overall abundance was subdominant, 10-40% of plant cover).
Snake River wheatgrass was a minor to subdominant component at two of the drill seeded plots.
Early senescence of perennial grasses made identification difficult especially for Snake River
wheatgrass which had dropped seeds and fully cured. It is likely that Snake River wheatgrass
abundance was higher than reported.

4. Qualitative increase in perennial grass and forb diversity compared to control area.
Conduct line point intercept monitoring and site assessment.
In 2017, there is a difference in diversity of perennial grass and forbs, plot G1UMT05 had
greater diversity; therefore, the objective is being met. Line-point intercept data indicated there
were 3 desirable perennial forbs and grasses at plot G1UMT03, 4 at G1UMT05, and 2 at
G1UMT06. The natural recovery plot had 2 desirable perennial grass and forb species. Species
richness from qualitative site assessments was similar at the drill seeded plots (5-6 species) and
the natural recovery plot (6 species).

Summary report 2022
Season of use for the treatment plots within the drill seeding is March 1 – March 26. Photos 8-1 and 8-2 were taken in May of 2022 near the four acre exclosure that was built in April of 2015 45 meters northwest of plot G1UMT06 (Photos 8-6).
In 2022 the drill seeded area has higher abundance of deep-rooted perennial grasses than the area that was left untreated (G1UMT04).

S3/R3 Aerial Seeding
This objective was not being met in 2022. Due to the lack of success of the aerial seeding a shrub restoration project is being implemented in fall of 2022.
CONCLUSIONS
In 2022 the drill seeding was somewhat successful in that drill seeded species were still present. However, cover and abundance of perennial grass species was too low to successfully outcompete cheatgrass, medusahead, and invasive annual forbs such as tall tumblemustard.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
FY 13
Monitoring plots were established during the summer of 2013. Cover and density transect data
were collected by ESR monitoring technicians (Tables 1-2). Cheatgrass cover and density across

seeded species occurred in early spring. Existing perennial grasses (crested wheatgrass) in the

currently low with the drill seeded species. The existing crested wheatgrass in the plant

Objectives: Establish perennial grasses and forbs within 3 years using a native dominated seed mix.
Actual_Implementation:
Approximately 34,706 acres were drill seeded starting in the fall of 2010 and completed in spring of 2011. ESR specialists monitored conditions and activities during treatment implementation.
This treatment consisted of five projects; Long Butte North, Long Butte Bombing Range, Long Butte Wild Horse Management Area, Long Butte South, and Long Butte Fuel Breaks (see attached map). Long Butte North consisted of 6,200 acres spread across approximately twelve separate blocks of land. The largest block was several thousand acres and the smallest plots were wildlife tracts of forty acres. The project started on November 1, 2010 with contractor Richard Barney and stopped on November 26th due to environmental conditions. The contractor continued seeding in the spring once conditions improved and was completed on February 21, 2011. The seed mix for this project was identified in the plan as the North Mix and consisted of Great Basin wildrye, bluebunch wheatgrass, Indian ricegrass, bottlebrush squirreltail, Siberian wheatgrass, globemallow, blue flax, and alfalfa.
Long Butte Bombing Range consisted of 3,180 acres in a single block of land. The project started on October 30, 2010 and was completed on November 4, 2010. Boise District BLM operations and fire staff provided personnel and equipment for the project. The seed mix for this project was North Mix.
Long Butte Wild Horse Management Area consisted of 20,326 acres in a single block of land. The project started on November 5, 2010 with Boise and Twin Falls District ESR, operations, and fire personnel. The project was stopped on November 29th due to environmental conditions. Personnel resumed seeding in the spring and completed the project on March 15, 2011. The seed mix for this project was North Mix.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results: Within the Long Butte North project area cheatgrass and sandberg bluegrass were the dominant vegetation throughout the seeded areas. Snake River wheatgrass, Great Basin wildrye, alfalfa, and Wyoming big sagebrush were detected in the southern block of the project area. Fire ecologists site visit during the summer noted the primary vegetation cover consisted of cheatgrass, sandberg bluegrass, and tumble mustard. Cheatgrass growth was extensive in some areas.\r\nCheatgrass and sandberg bluegrass dominated the cover in the Bombing Range project area but Snake River wheatgrass and bottlebrush squirreltail were detected in the both the cover transects and density frames. Alfalfa and sagebrush was also detected in the density frames.\r\nThe Wild Horse Management area is dominated by cheatgrass, crested wheatgrass, and sandberg bluegrass. Some alfalfa, Wyoming big sagebrush, bluebunch wheatgrass, bottlebrush squirreltail, and Great Basin wildrye were detected either in the cover transect or the density frames. A site visit by the fire ecologists during the summer noted the area appeared to primarily cheatgrass, sandberg bluegrass, with crested wheat seedings and some tumble mustard. In some parts of the area cheatgrass was thick and tall, up to three feet in height.
